intro: In this college you'll learn the Dutch you need for food and meals: name the three meals of the day, say what you like and dislike eating, talk about healthy and unhealthy food, plan a meal, and order politely in a café or restaurant.

paragraphs.heading: Welcome — food is everywhere
paragraphs.text: Welcome to theme four. Its title is just one happy little word: [[Lekker!]], which means 'Tasty!'. You will hear this word all day long in the Netherlands, because Dutch people use [[lekker]] for almost anything that feels good, not only food. But here we focus on eating and drinking, and that is a wonderful topic, because everyone eats, so you can practise your Dutch at the table, in the supermarket, and in every café. The first thing to know is the word for being hungry. You do not say 'I am hungry' word for word; instead you say [[Ik heb honger.]], literally 'I have hunger'. And for thirsty you say [[Ik heb dorst.]], 'I have thirst'. A very common family question at the end of the afternoon is [[Wat eten we vanavond?]], which means 'what are we eating tonight?'. As always in this college, I explain everything in clear English, but every Dutch word and sentence is spoken by a native Dutch voice, so you train your ear at the same time. Please repeat each phrase out loud after me — that is how the words really stick. Are you ready? [[Laten we beginnen!]]

paragraphs.heading: The three meals of the day
paragraphs.text: Let's start with the three meals. Breakfast is [[het ontbijt]], lunch is [[de lunch]], and the evening meal, dinner, is [[het avondeten]]. A typical Dutch breakfast and lunch are simpler than you might expect, because both are often just bread. The word for bread is [[brood]], and a single sandwich or roll is [[een broodje]]. So at midday many Dutch people eat [[een broodje kaas]], a cheese roll, with a glass of milk or [[karnemelk]], which is buttermilk. The warm meal of the day is usually in the evening. To talk about timing, you use the word [[om]] for 'at': for example [[Ik eet om zes uur.]], 'I eat at six o'clock'. A useful detail is that Dutch families often eat dinner early, around six, so do not be surprised if a Dutch friend invites you to dinner at that time. Some food words you need every day are [[de groente]], the vegetables; [[het fruit]], the fruit; [[het vlees]], the meat; [[de vis]], the fish; [[de kaas]], the cheese; and to drink, [[het water]]. Before anyone starts eating, Dutch people say the lovely phrase [[Eet smakelijk!]], which means 'enjoy your meal!'. Say it warmly and you sound truly local.

paragraphs.heading: Saying what you like and dislike
paragraphs.text: Now the heart of this theme: saying what you like and dislike. The key pattern is to start with 'I find', then the food, then the word for tasty. So 'I like cheese' becomes [[Ik vind kaas lekker.]] — literally 'I find cheese tasty'. The word [[lekker]] is doing the work there. For something you dislike, you keep the same shape but swap in the word for disgusting, [[vies]]. So [[Ik vind spruitjes vies.]] means 'I think Brussels sprouts are gross'. To ask another person, you say [[Vind je dat lekker?]], 'do you like that?'. There is also a special Dutch verb just for liking the taste of food: [[lusten]]. You will often hear the question [[Lust je vis?]], 'do you like (eating) fish?'. To say no, the natural answer is [[Ik lust geen vis.]], 'I don't like fish'. Notice that little word [[geen]], which means 'no' or 'not any' before a noun. And when something tastes really good while you are eating it, you can say [[Het smaakt heerlijk!]], 'it tastes delicious!', or [[Het is echt lekker.]], 'it's really tasty'. These few sentences let you have a real opinion at any table, so practise them with your own favourite and least favourite foods right now.

paragraphs.heading: Preferences: graag, liever, het liefst
paragraphs.text: Next, a small piece of grammar that makes you sound natural. To say you like doing something, Dutch does not use a separate verb for 'to like'; instead it adds the word [[graag]] to a normal sentence. So 'I like drinking coffee' becomes [[Ik drink graag koffie.]] — literally 'I drink gladly coffee'. To compare two things and say you prefer one, you use [[liever]], which means 'rather'. For example [[Ik eet liever vis dan vlees.]], 'I prefer fish to meat'. The pattern there joins two foods with [[liever]] before the first and [[dan]], meaning 'than', before the second. And for your absolute favourite, the top of the ladder, you use [[het liefst]], 'most of all'. So you might say [[Het liefst eet ik verse groente.]], 'most of all I like eating fresh vegetables'. Think of these three words as a neat staircase: [[graag]], then [[liever]], then [[het liefst]]. A waiter or a friend may ask [[Wat drink je het liefst?]], 'what do you most like to drink?'. You could answer [[Ik drink het liefst thee.]], 'I most like to drink tea'. Try building your own little ladder out loud: name a food you like with [[graag]], one you prefer with [[liever]], and your favourite with [[het liefst]].

paragraphs.heading: Healthy food and planning a meal
paragraphs.text: Let's talk about healthy eating and making a plan. The word for healthy is [[gezond]], and the opposite, unhealthy, is [[ongezond]]. So you can say [[Groente en fruit zijn gezond.]], 'vegetables and fruit are healthy', and [[Snoep en chips zijn ongezond.]], 'sweets and crisps are unhealthy'. The word [[snoep]] means sweets or candy. To say you try to eat healthily, a handy sentence is [[Ik probeer gezond te eten.]], 'I try to eat healthily'. When you plan a meal, you often go shopping first, [[boodschappen doen]], and then you cook, [[koken]]. A natural planning question between partners is [[Wat zullen we koken?]], 'what shall we cook?'. You can suggest a specific dish, for example [[Zullen we soep maken?]], 'shall we make soup?'. To say something is your turn to cook, you can say [[Vanavond kook ik.]], 'tonight I'm cooking'. And a small but useful word is [[lekker]] again inside a recipe context: [[Ik wil iets lekkers koken.]] means 'I want to cook something tasty'. Planning food together is one of the friendliest ways to use Dutch at home, so weave these phrases into your evenings.

paragraphs.heading: Eating out — and a café scene
paragraphs.text: Finally, eating out. When you sit down, ask for the menu with [[Mag ik de menukaart, alstublieft?]], 'may I have the menu, please?'. To order, the two most useful openers are [[Ik wil graag]], meaning 'I would like', and [[Mag ik]], meaning 'may I have'; you simply add the food after them. For example [[Ik wil graag de soep van de dag.]], 'I would like the soup of the day', or [[Mag ik een broodje kaas?]], 'may I have a cheese roll?'. For a drink you can simply say [[Voor mij een glas water, graag.]], 'a glass of water for me, please'. When you are finished and want to pay, the magic sentence is [[De rekening, alstublieft.]], which means 'the bill, please'. In the Netherlands friends often split the bill, and someone may send you a [[tikkie]], a quick little payment request on your phone. Let me leave you with a tiny scene. The waiter asks [[Hebben jullie al gekozen?]], 'have you chosen yet?'. You answer warmly: [[Ja, ik wil graag de tomatensoep.]] and [[Mag ik er een broodje kaas bij?]] At the end you smile and say [[Het was heel lekker, dank u.]], 'it was very tasty, thank you'. You can do this. [[Eet smakelijk, en tot de volgende keer!]]
